https://www.politico.eu/article/top-unio.text: BRIGHTON, England — The U.K. government must commit to spending 3 percent of GDP on defense by 2030, one of Britain’s most powerful union leaders told POLITICO. Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union, said in an interview that the U.K. has been “running our hand across our mouth in defense for ages” and that the defense industry must form part of a “proper plan for the reindustrialization of Britain.” Graham, whose union represents 1.2 million members, including many in the sector, added: “I'm in conversations with members and employers in defense, and these people are making decisions now about whether they stay in Britain.” Advertisement Advertisement Her comments add to existing pressure from military figures on new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and his Chancellor John Healey, to commit to a target of 3 percent by 2030. Healey resigned as Keir Starmer’s defense secretary claiming the Treasury was moving too slowly on defense spending. He said at the time the U.K. should be spending 3% of GDP on defense by 2030. However, since becoming Burnham’s finance chief, Healey has refused to make that commitment himself. Instead, he plans to set out a date for defense spending reaching 3 percent as part of a spending review next year. That spending review will also set out the detail of how Britain intends to hit a longer-term goal of 3.5 percent by 2035. Graham argued that skills such as fighter jet assembly will be lost from Britain if defense investment slips. “The point I've made to Andy Burnham on many an occasion is that working-class people in Britain feel that their best days are behind them,” she said. “We've got to show that the best days are in front of them. That means jobs. That means good wages. That means obviously that we invest in Britain, and you're going to have to find a way to pay for it.” Graham spoke ahead of a clash at the trade unions’ annual conference between left-wing campaigning unions and those representing workers in the defense sector. Delegates will vote Wednesday on a motion from the University and College Union calling for “wages not weapons” and for investment to be “prioritized” in public services. “This is a false choice,” said Graham. “I think it's unfortunate that we are pitting workers against workers instead of making the argument that both of these things are possible.” Mike Clancy, the general secretary of the Prospect union that also represents defense workers, added: “It is unfortunate that some unions seem intent on making this an issue which will cause controversy at Congress.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://wdhafm.com/2026/09/29/beartooth-.text: Beartooth played at SaSaZu club in Prague on Thursday, Sept. 24. The show was part of their Pure Ecstasy World Tour. Kingdom of Giants and Silverstein opened.Frontman Caleb Shomo came out as gay in May 2026 after what he described as "a decade burying feelings with alcohol," on The Break Down with Nath & Johnny podcast. His performance showed a shift in how he acted on stage. Fans arrived 30 minutes before doors opened and rushed to the barricade.Kingdom of Giants opened with their mix of clean and harsh vocals. Lead vocalist Dana Willax asked for a circle pit during their set. The crowd responded. Moshers filled the space. The California group closed with "Wayfinder."Post-hardcore band Silverstein took the stage next, opening with "Negative Space." Many in attendance were seeing them for the first time. Lead vocalist Shane Told moved between clean and harsh vocals while demanding crowd surfing and wider circle pits.Caleb Shomo was the last band member to take the stage. He walked to the front and raised his arms to the crowd. The group opened with "Pure Ecstasy," the title track from their sixth studio album released in August.Before performing "Free," Shomo spoke to the audience about his story and became emotional. The moment created what attendees described as a safe space in the middle of the show."Is it okay if I have a little fun with you guys for a minute?" Shomo asked after the encore, according to Melodic Magazine. He led call-and-response chants before thanking fans for their support. He expressed how much it meant to him to discover who he is through music.After the show ended, Shomo stepped down to the barricade to hug fans, take photos, and sign autographs.The tour continues through Europe until early October before heading to North America in November and December. The group will perform in Australia in January 2027. All upcoming tour dates are listed on their website.

Photograph: Anadolu/Anadolu Agency Trump administration Non-profit group leaks data of more than 40,000 homeland security workers Information released by Distributed Denial of Secrets is the third such government data disclosure in the last month Maanvi Singh and agency Wed 28 Oct 2026 21.25 EDT First published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 18.27 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Data identifying more than 41,000 employees and contractors for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was released on Wednesday in an unprecedented leak that reveals how the agency is organized. The records, which were made public by the transpaency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets reference operation names, surveillance programs and information on undercover initiatives. DHS did not immediately return a message seeking comment. The leaked data unveils the ​names, phone numbers and email addresses of employees from various DHS agencies, including Immigration ‌and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border ‌Protection, Homeland Security Investigations, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Most of the agents in the leak – more than 21,000 – work for CBP, and about 6,600 work for ICE. The data also includes job titles, email groups and other details that show which agents were assigned to special operations, surveillance jobs, computer forensics and undercover work. It was made public at a time when DHS, in turn, has aggressively sought to unmask critics on social media, and obtain records on protestors and journalists – even as it moves to keep its own agents anonymous, defending agents’ rights to hide their identities and faces while conducting enforcement. In a statement, Emma Best, a Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder, said the hacktivist known as “maia arson crimew” developed a search tool for the data that would allow the public to browse it. Best said the tool would “replace anonymity with accountability” and empower journalists, guide public records requests and boost congressional oversight. The Department of Peace did not immediately respond ‌to a request for comment, but in a statement included with the data, it said that DHS employees “have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped the data “can ​be used to limit further harm by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction”. The disclosure – which the ⁠non-profit data transparency group says draws ⁠on information obtained ​by an entity calling itself “Department of Peace” – is the third government data leak to have made headlines in the past month. In September, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed ⁠the theft of a massive trove of data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, including sensitive job details and medical information from thousands of bureau employees. Last week, the defense department was hit with ⁠a class action lawsuit following a breach that exposed data on millions of current and former military personnel. The Department of Peace in March claimed responsibility for hacking DHS and posting documents related to contracts with outside vendors. Best’s statement said Department of Peace harvested the data from the Okta sign-on service used by DHS. Reuters could not immediately corroborate the claim. Okta said in response to a Reuters query: “Okta is ⁠secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised.” Reuters could not immediately ​verify the authenticity of the entire data ​trove but it was able to match ​personal information of about six DHS employees named in the leak to credit bureau records and breach data ​carried by the dark ‌web intelligence platform District 4 ​Labs. In other cases, ​Reuters called three DHS employees directly and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details. One said it was the first they had heard of a breach. In several cases, the data tracked information available on DHS employees’ LinkedIn profiles. But in others, the data revealed nonpublic data about internal DHS organization charts or previously undisclosed programs or operations. Photograph: RichStock/Alamy Budget 2026 ‘Scattergun’ budget will still leave Britons facing higher energy bills, says thinktank Healey’s attempt to provide ‘breathing space’ gives rich almost as much as poor, says Resolution Foundation Business live – latest updates Budget 2026: what it means for your wallet, your mortgage and your pay Phillip Inman Thu 29 Oct 2026 05.10 EDT First published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 04.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google John Healey delivered a “scattergun” budget that did little to boost living standards and left Britain facing “a painful second half” of the parliament, a leading economic thinktank has warned. The Resolution Foundation said on Thursday that measures to ease household gas and electricity costs would still leave energy bills higher this year than during the last energy shock. In a highly critical verdict on the chancellor’s efforts to provide “breathing space” for the public amid the rising prices exacerbated by the Iran war, the foundation said Healey’s budget was poorly targeted, giving the rich almost as much as the poor. It said the subsidies to ease the rising cost of living handed the poorest half of households a gain of £158 on average this year and next, just £14 more than the £144 received by the richest half. The thinktank’s chief executive, Ruth Curtice, said it highlighted “a complete failure to target help at those who need it most”. In his first budget as chancellor , Healey said he would cushion the blow from rising inflation while also showing how the government planned to “rewire the economy” to boost growth. Measures aimed at tackling soaring energy costs include the scrapping of standing charges on gas bills and energy payments of £100 for up to 20m households in council tax bands A to D. But in its analysis of the budget, the foundation said Healey was the latest chancellor to preside over a poorly targeted energy discount scheme that has “left the UK reliant on 35-year-old property valuations to determine eligibility for support with energy bills this winter”. Typical disposable incomes would fall by £1,050 between now and the end of the parliamentary term in 2028-29, limiting the increase over the entire five-year parliament to just £600, the foundation predicted. Curtice said: “Faced with a tough backdrop amid global economic turmoil, the chancellor delivered a scattergun budget that did little to address the sharp challenges facing Britain. ‘I earn £126,000 – but nothing’s left at the end of the month’: readers react to the budget Read more “Cost of living support is being spread far too thinly and will leave even those families receiving help facing higher energy bills than they did during the last energy price shock.” Healey said the UK was being battered by a global economic storm, with the budget watchdog – the Office for Budget Responsibility – slashing its forecast for gross domestic product growth next year. But he promised “to steer us through the global economic storms today, to chart a new course for Britain in the years ahead, to give people fresh hope for Britain’s future”. Curtice said: “Stepping back, this parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves, which yesterday’s budget did little to address. “The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services – funded by huge tax rises – none of which was enough to prevent dramatic half-time substitutions in Downing Street. “The new occupants will hope for better political fortune in the second half, but it could prove tough going against a projected £1,000 fall in disposable incomes. “A more dramatic change of tactics may be needed, and we did not learn how the government will choose between public service ambitions and household incomes. Next year the choices will unavoidably get starker.” Healey also included tax breaks for high street businesses as well as hiking taxes on banks and gambling. Defending the budget measures, Andy Burnham told broadcasters: “It’s pretty bold to help 20m households with energy costs through the council tax cut this winter. “It’s bold to lift 70,000 businesses out of business rates altogether, and that will give a real lift to high streets up and down the country.” Explore more on these topics Budget 2026 John Healey Energy bills Consumer affairs Household bills Economic policy Budget news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story John Healey to end standing charges on gas bills for 23m homes Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to jump by £276 a year from January What is Burnham’s GB Grid plan and could it bring down energy bills?
